hook_text: In the 1990s South Africa had a national flower nobody planted: plastic bags on every fence.
clip_script: Drive through the Karoo in the late 1990s and every fence was draped in plastic. People called it the national flower. Why? The shopping bag is a few grams of polythene, so cheap shops gave away eight billion a year. Free, so you threw it away at once. Light, so it blew for kilometres. And it never rots, so wherever it landed, it stayed: fences, drains, rivers, turtles, cattle. In 2003 South Africa acted. Thin bags banned. Every bag charged for, with a levy for recycling. Use dropped by up to 80 percent. Fences cleared. Then the few cents stopped hurting, use crept back, and the levy money wandered. Biodegradable bags? Most only rot in a factory we do not have. The real fix turned out to be the woven bag you use fifty times. One cheap product, one law, one lesson: the use decides the impact, not the material.
visual_style: Whiteboard fence line fills with bag shapes, then clears after a 2003 stamp; a bar chart drops and creeps back; a woven bag with a tally of reuses appears last.
pacing: Problem in twenty seconds, law and results in twenty, alternatives and lesson in twenty.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and write the findings section of your own plastic-bag report.
